UI/UX Design

UI/UX Design: Why Good Design Sells — and How to Get It Right

What UI/UX design really is, why it directly affects sales and sign-ups, the process behind a good design, and the mistakes that quietly cost you customers.

NM Nipun Mitra ·26 October 2026 ·3 min read

UI/UX design decides whether people can actually use what you’ve built. You can have the best product, the best prices and great marketing, and still lose customers because the website is confusing, the checkout is long or the app hides the one button people need. Good design is not decoration — it’s one of the most direct levers you have on sales.

As a developer who turns Figma designs into production code every week, I see both sides: the design decisions that make a product easy to use, and the ones that look nice in a mockup but frustrate real users.

UI vs UX: what’s the difference?

  • UX (user experience) is how the product works: the structure, the steps to complete a task, what happens when something goes wrong.
  • UI (user interface) is how it looks and feels: layout, typography, colour, spacing, buttons and icons.

A beautiful interface on top of a confusing flow still fails. A clear flow with a messy interface feels untrustworthy. You need both working together.

Why good design sells

  • First impressions are visual. People judge credibility in seconds. A clean, consistent design signals a professional business.
  • Less friction, more conversions. Every extra field, unclear label or confusing step loses a percentage of people. Removing friction is often the cheapest growth you’ll find.
  • Fewer support requests. When the product explains itself, customers don’t need to call or message to ask how it works.
  • Higher retention. In apps and SaaS, people stay with tools that feel easy. Good onboarding and clear dashboards keep them coming back.

A practical UI/UX design process

  1. Understand users and goals. Who is this for, what are they trying to do, and what does the business need them to do?
  2. Map the user flows. Sketch the steps for the most important tasks — buying, booking, signing up, finding information.
  3. Wireframes. Simple grey boxes to agree on structure and content before anyone debates colours.
  4. High-fidelity design. Typography, colour, imagery and components in Figma, built on a small design system.
  5. Prototype and test. Click through the key flows with a few real users. Five people will reveal most of the big problems.
  6. Hand-off and build. Developers build from the design, keeping spacing and states consistent — including loading, empty and error states.

Design principles that make the biggest difference

  • One clear action per screen. Make the primary button obvious.
  • Visual hierarchy. Size, weight and spacing should tell people what to read first.
  • Consistency. The same component should look and behave the same everywhere.
  • Mobile first. Design for thumbs and small screens before large monitors.
  • Accessibility. Enough contrast, readable font sizes, labels on every field and visible focus states.
  • Feedback. Show what’s happening — loading indicators, success messages and helpful errors.

Common UI/UX mistakes that cost customers

  • Long forms that ask for information you don’t need yet.
  • Navigation labels that make sense internally but not to customers.
  • Tiny text and low-contrast grey on grey.
  • Pop-ups that cover the content as soon as the page loads.
  • Designs that look great on a desktop monitor and fall apart on a phone.
  • No clear next step at the end of a page.

Why design and development should work together

The best results come when design and development aren’t separate silos. A developer involved early can flag what will be slow or expensive to build; a designer involved during development keeps the details from drifting. That’s why I like to work from a shared design system and build components that match the Figma file one-to-one.

If you’re planning a new product or a redesign, take a look at my services — I’m happy to help with the design, the build, or both.

Frequently asked questions

What is the difference between UI and UX design?

UX (user experience) design is about how a product works — the flows, structure and ease of getting a task done. UI (user interface) design is how it looks — layout, typography, colour and components. Good products need both.

How does UI/UX design increase sales?

Clear navigation, readable pages, trust signals and short checkout or enquiry flows remove friction. When people can find what they need and act without confusion, more of them buy, book or get in touch.

Which tool is used for UI/UX design?

Figma is the most widely used tool today. It handles wireframes, high-fidelity designs, clickable prototypes and design systems, and developers can inspect designs directly when building them.
